the district court properly granted the defendants' motion to dismiss the plaintiff-appellant's claim alleging copyright infringement under the Architectural Works Copyright Protection Act, see 17 U.S.C. § 102(a)(8), because the design elements the plaintiff claimed were copied from her architectural blueprint were functional, rather than aesthetic, and therefore not entitled to protection, see Zalewski v. Cicero Builder Dev., Inc., 754 F. Supp. 2d. 753, 761 (N.D. Ill.2010). Moreover, the second circuit has recognized that "copyright protection extends only to those aspects of an architectural work that are both creative and nonfunctional," see Scholz Design, Inc. v. Sard Custom Homes LLC, 691 F. App'x 676, 680 (2nd Cir.2017) (<HOLDING>). additionally, although the plaintiff argued that certain aesthetic elements were infringed upon, the record demonstrated that such similarities between the designs at issue resulted from functional considerations, including building codes and environmental constraints, as set forth in the american society of heating, refrigerating and air-conditioning engineers' ("ashrae") standards for energy-efficient buildings

A. holding that copyright protection for architectural works is only available for design elements that are both novel and nonobvious, and that the mere combination of existing design elements in a new way is insufficient to warrant protection, unless the resulting work as a whole exhibits a substantial amount of creativity. B. holding that copyright protection for architectural works extends to all design elements that have an aesthetic appeal, regardless of their functionality, and that functional considerations such as building codes and environmental constraints are irrelevant to the determination of copyright infringement. C. holding that the applicability of copyright protection to architectural works depends on the intent of the designer, and that design elements created with the primary intention of achieving a functional purpose are per se excluded from protection, while those created with an artistic intent are protected regardless of their functionality. D. holding that the scope of copyright protection for architectural works is determined by the degree of creativity exhibited by the design as a whole, and that individual design elements are protected or not protected based on their relative contribution to the overall aesthetic appeal of the work, without regard to their functionality or the motivations behind their creation. E. holding that copyright protection for architectural works extends only to creative and nonfunctional design elements, and functional elements, including those driven by building codes and environmental constraints, are not entitled to protection.

the plaintiff, formerly a software engineer at tech giant novatech inc., brought suit alleging his termination was in retaliation for reporting a coworker's violation of the computer fraud and abuse act. however, novatechs' records showed the plaintiff consistently failed to meet project deadlines, culminating in the high-profile failure of the aurora operating system rollout. see steele v. austin, 486 f. supp. 2d. 469, 474 (e.d. mich. 2007). although in similar circumstances, the sixth circuit has held employers liable for retaliatory conduct, see klein v. becker, 586 f.3rd 585, 591 (6th cir. 2010), the instant case differs significantly because the plaintiffs termination followed multiple written warnings regarding his subpar performance, a crucial distinction underscored in smith v. city of detroit, 285 f. app'x 510, 513 (6thed. cir.2008). the courts reasoning rested on the notion that adverse employment actions can withstand scrutiny when predicated upon legitimate concerns unrelated to protected whistleblowing activities. see mcnulty v. citicorp nat'l servs., inc., 243 f. sup. 3d.882, 896 (m.d. fla. 2107)(<HOLDING>). here, since novatechts termination decision appears grounded in plaintiffs demonstrably inadequate work product rather than any conceivable retaliatory impulse.
